front: Why is std::vector the default container in C++, and what does its memory layout give you that a Python list does not?
back:
Answer. A vector is one contiguous heap buffer of T stored inline. v[i] is O(1), push_back is amortised O(1) because capacity grows geometrically, and insert or erase in the middle is O(n). A Python list holds pointers to separately allocated objects; a vector<double> is a flat array of doubles that the cache and vectorised loops stream through.

Code:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> v{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
    std::cout << "&v[1] - &v[0] = " << (&v[1] - &v[0]) << '\n';   // elements are adjacent
    v.push_back(4.0);      // amortised O(1); may reallocate and move every element
    std::cout << "size=" << v.size() << " capacity>=size: " << (v.capacity() >= v.size()) << '\n';
}
Output:
&v[1] - &v[0] = 1
size=4 capacity>=size: 1
Interview trap: a push_back that reallocates invalidates every iterator, pointer and reference into the vector. Reserve first when pointers must stay valid.

front: When is std::deque the right choice over std::vector, and what does it cost? Predict the output of this snippet.
back:
Answer. A deque gives O(1) push_front, pop_front, push_back and pop_back, and keeps O(1) random access. It is not one contiguous buffer: it is a sequence of fixed-size chunks behind an index, so iteration is slower than vector and elements are not contiguous across chunks.

Code:
#include <deque>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    std::deque<int> d{2, 3};
    d.push_front(1);                 // O(1) at the front
    d.push_back(4);                  // O(1) amortised at the back
    std::cout << "front=" << d.front() << " back=" << d.back() << '\n';
    std::cout << "d[2]=" << d[2] << " size=" << d.size() << '\n';
    for (int x : d) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
front=1 back=4
d[2]=3 size=4
1 2 3 4
Interview trap: using a deque as a path buffer gives up the contiguous layout that vectorised pricing loops want. Use a vector and a head index if you only pop from the front occasionally.
deque<int> after push_front(1) and push_back(4): elements span two chunks behind a map.

front: What does std::list give you that std::vector cannot, and what does it cost? Predict the output.
back:
Answer. Given an iterator to a node, insert and erase are O(1) and do not move other elements; other iterators stay valid; splice relinks nodes in O(1). It has no random access (no operator[]), and every node is a separate allocation, so iteration is cache-hostile.

Code:
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <list>

int main() {
    std::list<double> px{100.0, 101.0, 102.0};
    auto mid = std::next(px.begin());   // iterator to 101.0
    px.insert(mid, 100.5);              // O(1): no element moves
    px.push_front(99.0);                // O(1)
    px.erase(mid);                      // removes 101.0; other iterators stay valid
    for (double p : px) std::cout << p << ' ';
    std::cout << "\nsize=" << px.size() << '\n';
    // px[0];  // does not compile: std::list has no operator[]
}
Output:
99 100 100.5 102 
size=4
Interview trap: std::sort does not compile on a list because it needs random-access iterators; use the member px.sort(). For desk-sized data a sorted vector with a binary-search insert is often faster than a list because of locality.
std::list after insert, push_front and erase: separate linked nodes, final order 99, 100, 100.5, 102.

front: In C++, what does dv01["10Y"] do on a std::map when the key is missing? Predict the output and say why it is dangerous in risk code.
back:
Answer. operator[] inserts a value-initialised element (0.0 for a double) when the key is absent and returns a reference to it. A read has changed the container. Use find for a read where absence matters, or at, which throws std::out_of_range.

Code:
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <string>

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, double> dv01;
    dv01["5Y"] = 4.7;
    std::cout << "size=" << dv01.size() << '\n';
    double missing = dv01["10Y"];          // operator[] inserts a value-initialised 0.0
    std::cout << "missing=" << missing << " size=" << dv01.size() << '\n';
    auto it = dv01.find("30Y");            // find() never inserts
    std::cout << (it == dv01.end() ? "not found" : "found") << " size=" << dv01.size() << '\n';
}
Output:
size=1
missing=0 size=2
not found size=2
Interview trap: a missing tenor read through [] returns zero DV01 and is then summed as a real bucket, so the risk report silently understates the exposure. Use at() or find() wherever absence is a bug.
std::map after dv01["10Y"]: operator[] inserted a 0.0 node; find("30Y") ends at nullptr without inserting.

front: std::vector: operator[] is {{c1::O(1)}}; push_back is amortised {{c2::O(1)}}; inserting in the middle is {{c3::O(n)}}.
back:
Extra: std::list insert at a known iterator is O(1), but random access is O(n). std::map and std::set are O(log n) for find, insert and erase, and iterate in key order. std::unordered_map is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case.
Interview trap: an 'O(1) lookup' claim for unordered_map ignores the worst case from collisions and rehashing.

front: What is wrong with this loop? Predict what it prints under g++ -std=c++20 -Wall -Wextra -O2 and explain the mechanism.
back:
Buggy code:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> fills{5, -1, -1, 7};
    for (auto it = fills.begin(); it != fills.end(); ++it) {
        if (*it == -1) fills.erase(it);   // BUG: it is invalid after erase, then ++it
    }
    for (int f : fills) std::cout << f << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Actual output:
5 -1 7
Answer. erase(it) invalidates it and every iterator at or after the erased position, so ++it steps from an invalid iterator. The element after the first -1 slides into it, the loop steps past it, and the second -1 survives. The standard makes the whole loop undefined behaviour; this output is one manifestation, not a rule to rely on. Fix: take the iterator erase returns.
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> fills{5, -1, -1, 7};
    for (auto it = fills.begin(); it != fills.end();) {
        if (*it == -1) it = fills.erase(it);   // erase returns the next valid iterator
        else ++it;
    }
    for (int f : fills) std::cout << f << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
5 7
Interview trap: 'it worked in my test' is not evidence for erasing inside a raw loop. The modern one-liner is std::erase_if(fills, pred).

front: After std::vector::push_back reallocates, {{c1::all iterators, pointers and references}} into the vector are invalidated. For std::deque, push_front and push_back invalidate {{c2::all iterators but not references to existing elements}}.
back:
Extra: a vector push_back that does not reallocate invalidates only the end iterator. Insert and erase in the middle invalidate everything at or after the change point.
Interview trap: code that caches a pointer into a vector and keeps appending is a use-after-free that appears only when the capacity boundary is crossed; tests pass and production fails.
push_back that reallocates: the old buffer is freed, so a saved pointer into it dangles.

front: For std::list and std::map, erase invalidates only {{c1::iterators to the erased element}}, and insert invalidates {{c2::no iterators}}. For std::unordered_map, a rehash invalidates {{c3::all iterators but not references or pointers to elements}}.
back:
Extra: node-based containers never move their elements, so references and pointers survive insert and erase. The unordered_map rule is why a cached iterator is unsafe across inserts even though a cached element pointer is not.
Interview trap: caching &m.at(k) is safe across a rehash but caching m.begin() is not; reserve() before a bulk load avoids the rehash.

front: What is wrong with this code? Compile it with -fsanitize=address and state the report.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> ladder{100.0, 101.0};   // capacity exactly 2
    auto first = ladder.begin();
    ladder.push_back(102.0);                     // reallocates: old buffer is freed
    std::cout << *first << '\n';                 // BUG: first is dangling
}
Actual report: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-freeAnswer. The capacity of ladder is 2, so push_back allocates a new buffer and frees the old one; first still points into the freed memory, and dereferencing it is a use-after-free. Fix: take the iterator after the last mutation, or hold an index.
Interview trap: an invalid iterator is undefined behaviour, so it may print the old value on some builds. Reading a plausible value is not evidence the code is correct.

front: Does std::sort keep the arrival order of equal keys? Predict the output of this stability check and state the fix.
back:
Code:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

struct Trade { int id; int desk; };   // id = arrival order

// True if, within each desk, trades appear in arrival (id) order.
bool arrival_order_kept(const std::vector<Trade>& v) {
    for (std::size_t i = 1; i < v.size(); ++i)
        if (v[i - 1].desk == v[i].desk && v[i - 1].id > v[i].id) return false;
    return true;
}

int main() {
    std::vector<Trade> base;
    for (int id = 1; id <= 40; ++id) base.push_back({id, id % 3});   // desks 0, 1, 2

    std::vector<Trade> s = base;
    std::stable_sort(s.begin(), s.end(), [](const Trade& a, const Trade& b) { return a.desk < b.desk; });
    std::vector<Trade> u = base;
    std::sort(u.begin(), u.end(), [](const Trade& a, const Trade& b) { return a.desk < b.desk; });

    std::printf("stable_sort keeps arrival order within desk: %d\n", arrival_order_kept(s));
    std::printf("sort keeps arrival order within desk:        %d\n", arrival_order_kept(u));
    std::printf("first 6 of stable_sort:");
    for (int i = 0; i < 6; ++i) std::printf(" C%d", s[i].id);
    std::printf("\n");
}
Actual output:
stable_sort keeps arrival order within desk: 1
sort keeps arrival order within desk:        0
first 6 of stable_sort: C3 C6 C9 C12 C15 C18
Answer. std::sort is not stable and may reorder equal keys. std::stable_sort keeps the relative order, usually with extra memory. For a multi-key sort, the cleanest choice is one comparator on the full key, here (desk, id), with std::sort.
Interview trap: On libstdc++, std::sort on 16 or fewer elements is an insertion sort and so stays stable. The check above passes for 6 and 16 trades and fails for 17 and 40. A unit test on six trades passes; a realistic batch fails. Test at realistic sizes.

front: Write the zero-rate lookup for a curve with pillars t and zero rates z using std::lower_bound. Predict the four printed values.
back:
Answer. lower_bound returns the first pillar with t[i] >= x, so the bracketing segment is [i-1, i]; interpolate linearly in the rate, with flat extrapolation outside the pillars. By hand: at 0.5y the weight on the 1y pillar is (0.5-0.25)/0.75 = 1/3, so 4.10 - 0.1/3 = 4.0667; at 3.5y, 3.85 + 0.5 × (3.70 - 3.85) = 3.775.

Code:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

// Linear interpolation of a zero curve; t sorted ascending, flat extrapolation outside.
double interp(const std::vector<double>& t, const std::vector<double>& z, double x) {
    if (x <= t.front()) return z.front();
    if (x >= t.back())  return z.back();
    auto hi = std::lower_bound(t.begin(), t.end(), x);   // first pillar with t[i] >= x
    std::size_t i = static_cast<std::size_t>(hi - t.begin());
    double w = (x - t[i - 1]) / (t[i] - t[i - 1]);
    return z[i - 1] + w * (z[i] - z[i - 1]);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<double> t{0.25, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 10.0};
    std::vector<double> z{4.10, 4.00, 3.85, 3.70, 3.90};   // zero rates in %
    for (double x : {0.5, 2.0, 3.5, 12.0})
        std::printf("t=%.2f zero=%.4f\n", x, interp(t, z, x));
}
Output:
t=0.50 zero=4.0667
t=2.00 zero=3.8500
t=3.50 zero=3.7750
t=12.00 zero=3.9000
Interview trap: the front guard is what keeps i-1 from being -1, which is undefined behaviour. Linear interpolation of zero rates gives kinks in the forward curve; linear interpolation of log discount factors gives piecewise-flat forwards. Say which you use and why.

front: What does this print, and why?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> dv01{0.5, 0.25, 0.75};   // bucket risks
    double a = std::accumulate(dv01.begin(), dv01.end(), 0);     // init is int
    double b = std::accumulate(dv01.begin(), dv01.end(), 0.0);   // init is double
    std::cout << "int init:    " << a << '\n';
    std::cout << "double init: " << b << '\n';
}
Answer:
int init:    0
double init: 1.5
The accumulator has the type of the initial value. With 0 (an int), each partial sum is truncated back to an int, so 0.5, 0.25 and 0.75 all collapse to 0. With 0.0 the sum is 1.5.
Interview trap: there is no compiler warning and no exception. A port from Python that writes accumulate(v, 0) silently drops the fractional part of every DV01 bucket. Use 0.0 or a typed initial value.

front: Discount the cash flows of a 5% annual-coupon, 3-year bond at a flat 3% continuously compounded rate using std::transform. Predict the price per 100 face.
back:
Answer. DF(t) = exp(-r t), so each cash flow's PV is cf × DF. The first std::transform maps times to DFs (the back_inserter appends to an empty vector); the binary form multiplies cash flows by DFs. Check by hand: 5e^(-0.03) = 4.8522, 5e^(-0.06) = 4.7088, 105e^(-0.09) = 95.9628; sum 105.524.

Code:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <iostream>
#include <iterator>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const double r = 0.03;                        // flat continuously compounded rate
    std::vector<double> t{1.0, 2.0, 3.0};         // payment times in years
    std::vector<double> cf{5.0, 5.0, 105.0};      // 5% coupon bond cash flows
    std::vector<double> df;
    df.reserve(t.size());
    std::transform(t.begin(), t.end(), std::back_inserter(df),
                   [r](double ti) { return std::exp(-r * ti); });
    std::vector<double> pv(cf.size());
    std::transform(cf.begin(), cf.end(), df.begin(), pv.begin(),
                   [](double c, double d) { return c * d; });      // binary transform
    double price = std::accumulate(pv.begin(), pv.end(), 0.0);
    std::cout.precision(6);
    std::cout << "DF:    "; for (double d : df) std::cout << d << ' ';
    std::cout << "\nPV:    "; for (double p : pv) std::cout << p << ' ';
    std::cout << "\nPrice: " << price << '\n';
}
Output:
DF:    0.970446 0.941765 0.913931 
PV:    4.85223 4.70882 95.9628 
Price: 105.524
Interview trap: std::transform writes into the destination but does not resize it. Writing into df.begin() of an empty vector is undefined behaviour, which is why the code uses back_inserter or a pre-sized vector.

front: What is the annuity factor (PV01 per unit notional) for tenors 1 to 5 years at a flat 3% annual par rate, computed in one pass with std::partial_sum? Predict the table.
back:
Answer. The annual DF is 1/1.03^n and the annuity A(n) is the running sum of DFs, which is exactly what partial_sum computes. A(5) = 4.5797. Check: a flat 3% par curve must give par rate (1 - DF(5))/A(5) = (1 - 0.86261)/4.57970 = 3.000%.

Code:
#include <cmath>
#include <cstddef>
#include <iomanip>
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const double y = 0.03;                        // flat annual par yield
    std::vector<double> df;
    for (int n = 1; n <= 5; ++n) df.push_back(1.0 / std::pow(1.0 + y, n));   // DF(n years)
    std::vector<double> annuity(df.size());
    std::partial_sum(df.begin(), df.end(), annuity.begin());               // running sum
    std::cout << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4);
    for (std::size_t i = 0; i < df.size(); ++i)
        std::cout << i + 1 << "y  DF=" << df[i] << "  annuity=" << annuity[i] << '\n';
}
Output:
1y  DF=0.9709  annuity=0.9709
2y  DF=0.9426  annuity=1.9135
3y  DF=0.9151  annuity=2.8286
4y  DF=0.8885  annuity=3.7171
5y  DF=0.8626  annuity=4.5797
Used in the deck for: the annuity measure in par swap rate and swap PV01.
Interview trap: partial_sum is inclusive, so element i holds the sum through the (i+1)-th payment; the 1-year annuity is element 0, not element 1.

front: How do you read a 99% one-day VaR from 1,000 scenario P&Ls with std::nth_element instead of a full sort? Predict what it prints.
back:
Answer. A 99% VaR is the loss at the 1% quantile: with 1,000 scenarios, the 10th worst outcome, at 0-based index 9. nth_element places that value at index 9 with everything smaller on its left, in O(n) on average, rather than O(n log n) for a full sort. The sorted reference agrees (-491.0), so VaR = 491.0.

Code:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cstddef>
#include <cstdio>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    // 1000 deterministic, distinct daily P&L scenarios: {-500, ..., 499}
    std::vector<double> pnl;
    for (int i = 0; i < 1000; ++i) pnl.push_back(static_cast<double>((i * 37) % 1000) - 500.0);
    // 99% one-day VaR = loss at the 1% quantile = 10th worst of 1000 (0-based index 9)
    const std::size_t k = 9;
    std::vector<double> a = pnl;
    std::nth_element(a.begin(), a.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(k), a.end());
    std::vector<double> b = pnl;
    std::sort(b.begin(), b.end());
    std::printf("nth_element 10th worst P&L: %.1f\n", a[k]);
    std::printf("full sort   10th worst P&L: %.1f\n", b[k]);
    bool left_ok = std::all_of(a.begin(), a.begin() + static_cast<std::ptrdiff_t>(k),
                               [&](double x) { return x <= a[k]; });
    std::printf("left partition all <= q: %d\n", static_cast<int>(left_ok));
    std::printf("99%% 1-day VaR = %.1f\n", -a[k]);
}
Output:
nth_element 10th worst P&L: -491.0
full sort   10th worst P&L: -491.0
left partition all <= q: 1
99% 1-day VaR = 491.0
Interview trap: the off-by-one (index 10 is the 11th worst), the sign flip (VaR is quoted as a positive loss), and that a 99% figure from 1,000 scenarios rests on only 10 tail observations, so it is noisy.

front: How do you sort a vector of trades by quantity with C++20 ranges, without writing a comparator? Predict the output.
back:
Answer. std::ranges::sort(t, {}, &Trade::qty) takes the range directly and a projection (here a member pointer), with ranges::less as the comparator. The range overloads accept a container, not an iterator pair.

Code:
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>

struct Trade { std::string id; double qty; };

int main() {
    std::vector<Trade> t{{"A", 5.0}, {"B", -2.0}, {"C", 9.0}};
    std::ranges::sort(t, {}, &Trade::qty);     // sort by a projection, no lambda needed
    for (const auto& x : t) std::cout << x.id << ' ' << x.qty << '\n';
}
Output:
B -2
A 5
C 9
Interview trap: the projection is applied during comparison; it is not stored. Use it for readability, not as a cache. ranges::sort still needs random-access iterators (next card).

front: std::sort requires {{c1::random-access}} iterators, which is why std::list provides its own {{c2::sort()}} member function.
back:
Extra: introsort needs O(1) jumps to the middle of a range. A list merge sort rearranges nodes in place instead.
Interview trap: a list-based code path that calls std::sort fails to compile. The fix is the member sort, not a silent copy into a vector unless that copy is cheap.

front: What do by_value() and by_ref() return after notional = 250? Explain the capture rule.
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int notional = 100;
    auto by_value = [notional] { return notional; };     // copies now
    auto by_ref   = [&notional] { return notional; };    // refers to the variable
    notional = 250;
    std::cout << "by value: " << by_value() << '\n';
    std::cout << "by ref:   " << by_ref() << '\n';
}
Output:
by value: 100
by ref:   250
Answer. A capture by value copies the variable when the lambda is created, so the closure keeps 100. A capture by reference stores a reference to the variable, so it sees 250.
Interview trap: [=] inside a member function captures the this pointer, not the object, so a lambda that outlives the object reads freed memory. C++20 deprecates implicit capture of this by [=]. Capture what you name.
By-value capture keeps the copy made at creation (100); by-reference capture sees the variable (250).

front: What is wrong with make_pricer? State the sanitizer report, then give the fix and its output.
back:
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>

std::function<double()> make_pricer(double spot) {
    double bump = 0.01 * spot;
    return [&] { return spot + bump; };      // captures locals by reference
}

int main() {
    auto f = make_pricer(100.0);
    std::cout << f() << '\n';                // BUG: spot and bump no longer exist
}
Actual report: AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-return (with ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_stack_use_after_return=1)
Answer. [&] captures spot and bump by reference. Both are locals that die when make_pricer returns, but the returned std::function keeps the references. Fix: capture by value.
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>

std::function<double()> make_pricer(double spot) {
    double bump = 0.01 * spot;
    return [spot, bump] { return spot + bump; };   // capture by value
}

int main() {
    auto f = make_pricer(100.0);
    std::cout << f() << '\n';
}
Output:
101
Interview trap: std::function copies the closure, not the storage it refers to. A stored lambda with reference captures is safe only while its referents live; for anything kept past the call, capture values.

front: Each leg in this vector is meant to return 90, 100 and 110. What does it return, and what does the sanitizer report?
back:
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::function<double()>> legs;
    for (double k : {90.0, 100.0, 110.0})
        legs.push_back([&k] { return k; });        // BUG: captures the loop variable by reference
    for (auto& leg : legs) std::cout << leg() << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Actual report: AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope. Without a sanitizer, this build at -O2 prints 110 110 110, not 90 100 110: the reads go to dead storage, so the value is undefined.
Answer. The range-for variable k is a fresh local each iteration, destroyed at the end of it. The lambda captured its address, so each call reads dead storage. Fix: capture by value, [k].
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<std::function<double()>> legs;
    for (double k : {90.0, 100.0, 110.0})
        legs.push_back([k] { return k; });        // capture by value
    for (auto& leg : legs) std::cout << leg() << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
90 100 110
Interview trap: the same bug appears with [&] when building callbacks for a scenario grid. The build is clean under -Wall -Wextra, so the first sign is wrong numbers or a crash.

front: Predict the output. Why does next_id need mutable, and why does counter still print 0?
back:
#include <iostream>

int main() {
    auto next_id = [id = 1000]() mutable { return id++; };   // init-capture plus mutable state
    std::cout << next_id() << ' ' << next_id() << ' ' << next_id() << '\n';
    int counter = 0;
    auto bump = [counter]() mutable { return ++counter; };   // mutates its own copy
    std::cout << bump() << ' ' << bump() << ' ' << counter << '\n';
}
Output:
1000 1001 1002
1 2 0
Answer. The init-capture id = 1000 creates a member of the closure. The call operator is const by default, so changing id needs mutable. The closure's own copy changes; the variable counter in main never does.
Interview trap: a stateful lambda is copied when passed by value or wrapped in std::function, and each copy has its own state. A lambda used as a shared id counter is not shared between copies.

front: A trapezoid integrator takes a callback. Compare a template parameter with a std::function parameter for a quadrature or Monte Carlo inner loop. Predict the printed values.
back:
#include <cmath>
#include <functional>
#include <iostream>

// Template: F is known at compile time, call is inlinable, no allocation.
template <class F>
double trap_tpl(F f, double a, double b, int n) {
    double h = (b - a) / n, s = 0.5 * (f(a) + f(b));
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) s += f(a + i * h);
    return s * h;
}

// std::function: type-erased, indirect call, may heap-allocate the callable.
double trap_fn(const std::function<double(double)>& f, double a, double b, int n) {
    double h = (b - a) / n, s = 0.5 * (f(a) + f(b));
    for (int i = 1; i < n; ++i) s += f(a + i * h);
    return s * h;
}

int main() {
    auto g = [](double x) { return std::exp(-x * x); };
    std::cout.precision(10);
    std::cout << "template: " << trap_tpl(g, 0.0, 1.0, 1000) << '\n';
    std::cout << "function: " << trap_fn(g, 0.0, 1.0, 1000) << '\n';
}
Output:
template: 0.7468240715
function: 0.7468240715
Answer. Both print 0.7468240715, the trapezoid rule with 1,000 steps. The exact value is (√π/2)·erf(1) ≈ 0.7468241328, so the error is about -6×10⁻⁸, as the h²/12 error term predicts. The template version inlines the lambda and allocates nothing. std::function is type-erased and calls indirectly, and may allocate. Use the template in the hot loop; use std::function at a configuration boundary such as stored callbacks or plug-in models.
Interview trap: passing a lambda to a const std::function& parameter builds a temporary std::function at every call, so doing it inside a loop turns one conversion into one per iteration.

front: What does quote return for a missing key, and what happens when value() is called on it? Predict each printed line.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <map>
#include <optional>
#include <string>

std::optional<double> quote(const std::map<std::string, double>& book, const std::string& id) {
    auto it = book.find(id);
    if (it == book.end()) return std::nullopt;
    return it->second;
}

int main() {
    std::map<std::string, double> book{{"BOND_A", 99.25}};
    auto a = quote(book, "BOND_A");
    auto b = quote(book, "BOND_B");
    std::cout << a.value_or(-1.0) << ' ' << b.value_or(-1.0) << '\n';
    std::cout << (b ? "has value" : "empty") << '\n';
    try {
        std::cout << b.value() << '\n';
    } catch (const std::bad_optional_access& e) {
        std::cout << "value() threw: " << e.what() << '\n';
    }
}
Output:
99.25 -1
empty
value() threw: bad optional access
Answer. std::optional<double> models 'a double or nothing' without a sentinel. value_or supplies a fallback; value() throws std::bad_optional_access; *opt on an empty optional is undefined behaviour.
Interview trap: returning -1 as 'no quote' is a sentinel that becomes a real price the first time someone sums or compares. Use optional and make the empty path explicit at the call site.

front: Price the DV01 of a mixed book of a bond, a swap and a cash position with std::variant and std::visit. What does the program print?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <variant>
#include <vector>

struct Bond { double face; double mod_dur; };      // DV01 = face * mod_dur * 1e-4
struct Swap { double notional; double annuity; };  // DV01 = notional * annuity * 1e-4
struct Cash { double amount; };                    // no rate sensitivity

template <class... Ts> struct overloaded : Ts... { using Ts::operator()...; };
template <class... Ts> overloaded(Ts...) -> overloaded<Ts...>;

using Position = std::variant<Bond, Swap, Cash>;

double dv01(const Position& p) {
    return std::visit(overloaded{
        [](const Bond& b) { return b.face * b.mod_dur * 1e-4; },
        [](const Swap& s) { return s.notional * s.annuity * 1e-4; },
        [](const Cash&)   { return 0.0; },
    }, p);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<Position> book{Bond{10'000'000, 4.5}, Swap{50'000'000, 4.1}, Cash{1'000'000}};
    double total = 0.0;
    for (const auto& p : book) total += dv01(p);
    std::cout << "index of Swap: " << book[1].index() << '\n';
    std::cout << "total DV01 = " << total << '\n';
    if (auto* s = std::get_if<Swap>(&book[1])) std::cout << "swap notional " << s->notional << '\n';
    std::cout << "holds Bond? " << std::holds_alternative<Bond>(book[1]) << '\n';
}
Output:
index of Swap: 1
total DV01 = 25000
swap notional 5e+07
holds Bond? 0
Answer. A variant holds exactly one of its alternatives: a type-safe tagged union. std::visit calls the handler for the active alternative; the overloaded idiom (lambdas plus a deduction guide) gives one handler per alternative. Check: 10,000,000 × 4.5 × 1e-4 = 4,500 and 50,000,000 × 4.1 × 1e-4 = 20,500; total 25,000. index() is 1 because the swap is the second alternative. The default stream format printed the notional as 5e+07; use std::fixed for desk output.
Interview trap: index() depends on declaration order, so reordering the alternatives silently changes any code that switches on indices. Prefer std::visit or get_if; std::get throws std::bad_variant_access on the wrong alternative.

front: For a type with a constructor, what is the difference between v.push_back(Trade{...}) and v.emplace_back(...)? Predict the output.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <utility>
#include <vector>

struct Trade {
    std::string id;
    double qty;
    Trade(std::string i, double q) : id(std::move(i)), qty(q) { std::cout << "ctor " << id << '\n'; }
    Trade(const Trade& o) : id(o.id), qty(o.qty) { std::cout << "copy " << id << '\n'; }
    Trade(Trade&& o) noexcept : id(std::move(o.id)), qty(o.qty) { std::cout << "move\n"; }
};

int main() {
    std::vector<Trade> v;
    v.reserve(4);                      // no reallocation below, so no extra moves
    std::cout << "push_back:\n";
    v.push_back(Trade{"T1", 5.0});     // builds a temporary, then moves it in
    std::cout << "emplace_back:\n";
    v.emplace_back("T2", 7.0);         // constructs in place from the arguments
    std::cout << "size=" << v.size() << '\n';
}
Output:
push_back:
ctor T1
move
emplace_back:
ctor T2
size=2
Answer. push_back takes a T&&, so the caller builds a temporary and the vector moves it in: construct, then move. emplace_back forwards the arguments and constructs the element in the vector's storage: one construction, no move. The output shows ctor then move for push_back, and a single ctor for emplace_back.
Interview trap: emplace does not help if you already hold an object; it then copies. And a vector moves elements on growth only when the move constructor is noexcept; otherwise it copies, which is why reserve and a noexcept move both matter.

front: What is the difference between reserve(n) and resize(n) on a vector? What do the printed values show?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> a;
    a.reserve(3);                      // capacity only
    std::cout << "reserve: size=" << a.size() << " capacity>=3: " << (a.capacity() >= 3) << '\n';
    a.push_back(1.5);
    std::cout << "after push: size=" << a.size() << " a[0]=" << a[0] << '\n';
    std::vector<double> b;
    b.resize(3);                       // size 3, three zeros
    b.push_back(2.5);
    std::cout << "resize: size=" << b.size() << " b[0]=" << b[0] << " b[3]=" << b[3] << '\n';
}
Output:
reserve: size=0 capacity>=3: 1
after push: size=1 a[0]=1.5
resize: size=4 b[0]=0 b[3]=2.5
Answer. reserve changes capacity only; size stays 0. resize changes size and value-initialises the new elements to 0. After resize(3) and push_back(2.5), the vector holds three zeros followed by 2.5, which is why b[3] is 2.5.
Interview trap: the classic bug is to reserve and then index the vector as if it had elements. That is the next card.

front: What is wrong with this code? State the assertion that -D_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS reports and the fix.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> marks;
    marks.reserve(3);            // capacity 3, size 0
    marks[0] = 1.5;              // BUG: operator[] needs size > 0, not capacity
    std::cout << marks[0] << '\n';
}
Reported: Assertion '__n < this->size()' failed
Answer. reserve(3) allocates capacity but leaves size at 0, and operator[] requires an index below size. Writing marks[0] is undefined behaviour; without the assertion it may appear to work. Fix: push_back(1.5), or construct with std::vector<double> marks(3), or resize(3).
Interview trap: Python has no separate capacity, so this bug has no direct analogue. In C++ capacity is an allocation detail; size is what indexing sees.

front: std::optional<T> stores the value {{c1::inline, with no heap allocation}}. value() throws {{c2::std::bad_optional_access}} on an empty optional, and value_or(x) returns {{c3::x}} in that case.
back:
Extra: *opt on an empty optional is undefined behaviour, not an exception.
Interview trap: if (opt) followed by *opt is fine; *opt without the check is undefined behaviour, which the compiler will not flag.

front: What does std::remove do to a vector, what does the erase-remove idiom add, and what is the C++20 replacement? Predict the printed sizes.
back:
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<int> v{1, -1, 2, -1, 3};
    std::vector<int> r = v;
    auto new_end = std::remove(r.begin(), r.end(), -1);   // shifts survivors, size unchanged
    std::cout << "after remove alone: size=" << r.size() << '\n';
    r.erase(new_end, r.end());                             // erase-remove idiom
    std::vector<int> b = v;
    std::erase(b, -1);                                     // C++20 free function
    std::vector<int> c = v;
    std::erase_if(c, [](int x) { return x < 0; });
    std::cout << "idiom: size=" << r.size() << " std::erase: size=" << b.size()
              << " erase_if: size=" << c.size() << '\n';
    for (int x : c) std::cout << x << ' ';
    std::cout << '\n';
}
Output:
after remove alone: size=5
idiom: size=3 std::erase: size=3 erase_if: size=3
1 2 3
Answer. std::remove shifts the kept elements forward and returns the new logical end. It does not change the size, so the tail still holds moved-from values. v.erase(new_end, v.end()) removes the tail. C++20 provides std::erase(v, value) and std::erase_if(v, pred), which do both steps.
Interview trap: never read past the new end after std::remove; those elements are valid but unspecified.

front: Why take std::span<const double> rather than const std::vector<double>&? Predict the four printed values.
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

double total(std::span<const double> xs) {
    return std::accumulate(xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0.0);
}

int main() {
    std::vector<double> pnl{1.0, -2.0, 3.5, 0.5, 4.0};
    double buckets[3] = {10.0, 20.0, 30.0};
    std::cout << total(pnl) << '\n';                                          // no copy
    std::cout << total(std::span<const double>(pnl).subspan(1, 3)) << '\n';   // view of 3 elements
    std::cout << total(buckets) << '\n';                                      // C array works too
    std::cout << "size=" << std::span<const double>(pnl).size() << '\n';
}
Output:
7
2
60
size=5
Answer. A span is a non-owning pointer plus a size. It accepts a vector, a C array or a subrange with no copy and no allocation. subspan(1, 3) is -2, 3.5, 0.5, which sums to 2.
Interview trap: a span does not extend the lifetime of what it views. The next card shows where that bites.

front: What is wrong with this program? Compile with -fsanitize=address and state the report. Why does the compiler accept it?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <numeric>
#include <span>
#include <vector>

double total(std::span<const double> xs) {
    return std::accumulate(xs.begin(), xs.end(), 0.0);
}

std::vector<double> make_pnl() { return {1.0, -2.0, 3.5}; }

int main() {
    std::span<const double> view = make_pnl();   // BUG: the vector is destroyed at the end of this line
    std::cout << total(view) << '\n';
}
Actual report: AddressSanitizer: heap-use-after-free
Answer. make_pnl() returns a temporary vector, which is destroyed at the end of the declaration. The element type is const double, and the C++20 span constructor accepts rvalue ranges for const element types, so the view points at freed memory without any compile error. Fix: keep the vector in a named variable for the span's lifetime.
Interview trap: the same bug appears with std::string_view s = std::string(...), and with functions returning a span of a local vector.

front: Predict the three printed lines. Which conversions truncate and which promote?
back:
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std::chrono;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    seconds t{90};
    minutes m = duration_cast<minutes>(t);      // explicit cast: 1.5 min truncates to 1
    milliseconds ms = t + 250ms;                 // common type of seconds and milliseconds
    std::cout << m.count() << " min, " << ms.count() << " ms\n";
    duration<double, std::milli> d = 1.5s;      // floating-point duration keeps the fraction
    std::cout << d.count() << " ms\n";
    std::cout << duration_cast<seconds>(2500ms).count() << " s\n";
}
Output:
1 min, 90250 ms
1500 ms
2 s
Answer. duration_cast to an integer duration truncates toward zero: 90 s to minutes is 1. Adding seconds to milliseconds promotes to the common type, milliseconds. The 1.5s literal is a floating-point duration, so converting it to a floating millisecond duration keeps the fraction: 1500 ms.
Interview trap: measure elapsed time with std::chrono::steady_clock; system_clock can jump when the wall clock is adjusted.

front: Why does this not compile? State the compiler error and show an explicit conversion that does.
back:
#include <chrono>

using namespace std::chrono;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    seconds s = 1.5s;    // does not compile: a floating-point duration would silently lose 0.5 s
    return static_cast<int>(s.count());
}
Actual compiler error: conversion from ‘duration<long double>’ to non-scalar type ‘duration<long int>’ requested
Answer. A floating-point duration does not convert implicitly to an integer tick count, because the fraction would be lost silently; the compiler forces an explicit cast. Fixed version:
#include <chrono>
#include <iostream>

using namespace std::chrono;
using namespace std::chrono_literals;

int main() {
    seconds s = duration_cast<seconds>(1.5s);            // explicit: truncates 1.5 s to 1 s
    milliseconds ms = duration_cast<milliseconds>(1.5s);
    std::cout << s.count() << " s, " << ms.count() << " ms\n";
}
Output:
1 s, 1500 ms
Interview trap: duration_cast truncates. For rounding use std::chrono::round (C++17) or a finer unit; a timestamp truncated to whole seconds is a silent error.

front: Predict the output. Are two mt19937_64 engines with the same seed reproducible, and what does a default-constructed mt19937 produce?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <random>

int main() {
    std::mt19937_64 g1(42), g2(42), g3(43);
    std::cout << "g1 first: " << g1() << '\n';
    std::cout << "g2 first: " << g2() << '\n';
    std::cout << "g3 first: " << g3() << '\n';
    std::mt19937 d;                     // default-constructed: fixed seed 5489, not random
    std::cout << "default mt19937 first: " << d() << '\n';
}
Output:
g1 first: 13930160852258120406
g2 first: 13930160852258120406
g3 first: 517903087452778646
default mt19937 first: 3499211612
Answer. The Mersenne Twister engine is deterministic: the same seed gives the same sequence on any conforming implementation. The first two lines match and the third differs. A default-constructed mt19937 uses the fixed seed 5489, so its first output is the same on every run.
Interview trap: a default-constructed engine is not random. A simulation that forgets to seed gives the same paths every run, which looks like stability. Seed from std::random_device in production and log the seed; do not assume std::random_device is non-deterministic on every platform.

front: A regression test expects the first three normal draws from seed 2026 to be fixed. What does this print with g++ and libstdc++, and what could make it differ on another machine?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <random>

int main() {
    std::mt19937_64 gen(2026);
    std::normal_distribution<double> z(0.0, 1.0);
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) std::cout << z(gen) << '\n';
}
Output:
1.10955
-1.31188
1.6161
Answer. The engine's output is exactly specified by the standard, but std::normal_distribution (and the uniform distributions) are not: their algorithms are implementation-defined, so libstdc++, libc++ and MSVC may produce different sequences from the same engine state. The values printed are libstdc++ values.
Interview trap: a P&L or VaR regression that passes on Linux can drift on a Windows build for this reason alone. Either pin the standard library, or generate the normal from the engine's uniform output yourself (Box–Muller or inverse CDF) so the transform lives in your code.

front: Write a GBM Monte Carlo price for a European call (S0 = K = 100, r = 3%, σ = 20%, T = 1, 200,000 paths) and check it against Black–Scholes. What is printed?
back:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <random>

int main() {
    const double S0 = 100.0, K = 100.0, r = 0.03, sigma = 0.20, T = 1.0;
    const int N = 200000;
    std::mt19937_64 gen(2026);                        // one engine, reused for every path
    std::normal_distribution<double> z(0.0, 1.0);
    double sum = 0.0, sumsq = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        double ST = S0 * std::exp((r - 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T + sigma * std::sqrt(T) * z(gen));
        double payoff = std::exp(-r * T) * std::max(ST - K, 0.0);
        sum += payoff;
        sumsq += payoff * payoff;
    }
    double mean = sum / N;
    double var = (sumsq / N - mean * mean) * N / (N - 1);   // unbiased sample variance
    double se = std::sqrt(var / N);
    auto Phi = [](double x) { return 0.5 * std::erfc(-x / std::sqrt(2.0)); };
    double d1 = (std::log(S0 / K) + (r + 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T) / (sigma * std::sqrt(T));
    double d2 = d1 - sigma * std::sqrt(T);
    double bs = S0 * Phi(d1) - K * std::exp(-r * T) * Phi(d2);
    std::printf("MC  = %.4f +/- %.4f (1 s.e.)\n", mean, se);
    std::printf("BS  = %.4f\n", bs);
}
Output:
MC  = 9.3705 +/- 0.0314 (1 s.e.)
BS  = 9.4134
Answer. Simulate \( S_T = S_0\exp\big((r-\tfrac12\sigma^2)T+\sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z\big) \), average \( e^{-rT}(S_T-K)^+ \), and report the sample standard error. Black–Scholes gives 9.4134 and the MC estimate is 9.3705 ± 0.0314; the 0.043 gap is about 1.4 standard errors, which is consistent.
Interview trap: the error scales as \( 1/\sqrt{N} \), so each extra decimal place costs 100 times the paths. Quote the standard error with every MC price; a price without an error bar is not a result.

front: What is wrong with this Monte Carlo loop? Predict the printed standard error.
back:
#include <algorithm>
#include <cmath>
#include <cstdio>
#include <random>

int main() {
    const double S0 = 100.0, K = 100.0, r = 0.03, sigma = 0.20, T = 1.0;
    const int N = 10000;
    double sum = 0.0, sumsq = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        std::mt19937_64 gen(12345);                   // BUG: re-seeded on every path
        std::normal_distribution<double> z(0.0, 1.0);
        double ST = S0 * std::exp((r - 0.5 * sigma * sigma) * T + sigma * std::sqrt(T) * z(gen));
        double payoff = std::exp(-r * T) * std::max(ST - K, 0.0);
        sum += payoff;
        sumsq += payoff * payoff;
    }
    double mean = sum / N;
    double se = std::sqrt(std::max(0.0, sumsq / N - mean * mean) / N);
    std::printf("estimate = %.4f, s.e. = %.6f\n", mean, se);
}
Output:
estimate = 0.0000, s.e. = 0.000000
Answer. The engine is constructed inside the loop with a fixed seed, so every path draws the same Z. All payoffs are identical, the sample variance is zero, and the standard error is zero. The estimate of 0 is only because that one draw is out of the money; another seed would give a different estimate with the same zero error bar. Fix: construct the engine once, outside the loop.
Interview trap: a standard error of exactly zero on a path-dependent estimate is always a bug, not precision. Assert that s.e. is positive in tests.

front: std::mt19937 produces {{c1::32-bit}} outputs and std::mt19937_64 produces {{c2::64-bit}} outputs; the Mersenne Twister period is {{c3::219937 - 1}}.
back:
Extra: the state is 624 words for mt19937 and 312 words for mt19937_64. Copying an engine copies its state, so the copy replays the same sequence.
Interview trap: a parallel Monte Carlo that copies one engine to every thread gives identical, perfectly correlated paths. Give each thread its own independent seed or stream.

front: Predict the output. Why does changing pnl[0] after the view is built change the result?
back:
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    std::vector<double> pnl{-3.0, 2.0, -1.5, 4.0, 0.5};
    auto losses = pnl | std::views::filter([](double x) { return x < 0; })
                      | std::views::transform([](double x) { return -x; });
    pnl[0] = -10.0;                      // views are lazy: the change is visible
    for (double l : losses) std::cout << l << ' ';
    std::cout << "\ncount=" << std::ranges::distance(losses) << '\n';
}
Output:
10 1.5 
count=2
Answer. Range views are lazy: filter and transform refer to the source and compute each element when iterated. Nothing is copied when the view is built. After pnl[0] = -10 the first loss is 10; the losses are 10 and 1.5, a count of 2.
Interview trap: ranges::distance on a filtered view walks the whole range, and each pass re-runs the predicate. Iterating a view repeatedly in a hot loop costs the predicate times the number of passes.

front: What is the type of it here, and why is that useful? Predict the output.
back:
#include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <ranges>
#include <type_traits>
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> make() { return {1, 2, 3, 4}; }

int main() {
    auto it = std::ranges::find(make(), 3);     // the temporary dies, so no iterator is returned
    std::cout << "result is ranges::dangling: "
              << std::is_same_v<decltype(it), std::ranges::dangling> << '\n';
    auto v = std::vector{1, 2, 3, 4};
    auto ok = std::ranges::find(v, 3);          // lvalue: a real iterator
    std::cout << *ok << '\n';
}
Output:
result is ranges::dangling: 1
3
Answer. The range argument is a temporary, so the algorithm returns std::ranges::dangling instead of an iterator into a vector that dies at the end of the full expression. Dereferencing it does not compile. The lvalue version returns a real iterator.
Interview trap: ranges::dangling guards only the return value of an algorithm. An iterator copied out of a container variable that is destroyed first is still a use-after-free.
